text: Connectivity and identity still leave a gap. Once an enterprise has servers scattered across on-prem and multiple clouds, plus a handful of Kubernetes clusters, there's no single pane of glass for patching, policy, inventory, and access — each side drifts apart on its own tooling. This lesson covers the two real technologies built specifically to close that gap: Azure Arc and AWS Outposts, and they solve it from genuinely opposite directions.

Azure Arc extends Azure's control plane outward to infrastructure you already own. Install the Connected Machine agent on a server anywhere — on-prem, in AWS, in Google Cloud — and it registers in Azure as a resource, reachable by Azure Policy, Defender for Cloud, and Monitor. Arc-enabled Kubernetes does the same for any CNCF-conformant cluster, adding GitOps configuration through Flux and governance through Azure Policy for Kubernetes. Arc-enabled data services bring that same experience to SQL Server and SQL Managed Instance. Nothing about the underlying hardware changes — it's purely a software layer giving Azure visibility and governance.

In practice, onboarding looks like running azcmagent connect on the server itself, pointing it at a resource group, tenant, and subscription. From that point on, az connectedmachine show and every other Azure CLI command that targets a resource works against it, exactly as if it were a native Azure VM — except it never left your building.

AWS Outposts takes the opposite approach: instead of software reaching out, AWS ships you actual hardware — an Outposts rack or a compact 1U or 2U server — installed physically in your own data center or colo. Once it's running, you provision EC2 instances, EBS volumes, and on the rack form factor even RDS and EKS, through the exact same APIs, CLI, and console as AWS proper. That matters specifically for latency-sensitive and data-residency workloads: you get AWS-native compute right next to the data, managed by AWS as an extension of your home Region.

Launching an instance on an Outpost uses ordinary EC2 syntax — run-instances with an image, instance type, and subnet, no special API. The only real difference is that the subnet you target carries an outpost ARN, which is what routes the request to physical hardware sitting in your building instead of a Region's data center.

So: Arc extends Azure's management reach to infrastructure you already have, and Outposts brings genuine AWS hardware to you — structurally different answers to the same hybrid-management problem, and both worth knowing which one actually fits. Next lesson turns everything from this chapter into an actual decision framework: a practical way to decide what should stay on-premises and what should move to the cloud.
